stem:
Dahlia sold pineapples at a fruit stand. The table shows the number of pineapples Dahlia had for sale each week and the number of customers she expected to come to her fruit stand.

Dahlia’s Pineapples

|                     | Week 1 | Week 2 | Week 3 | Week 4 |
|---------------------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Number of Pineapples | 110    | 150    | 200    | 25     |
| Number of Expected Customers | 50     | 150    | 40     | 50     |

In which week did Dahlia most likely sell her pineapples for the highest price?

options.label: F
options.text: Week 1, because the number of pineapples was greater than the expected number of customers

options.label: G
options.text: Week 2, because the number of pineapples was the same as the expected number of customers

options.label: H
options.text: Week 3, because fewer customers were expected to come to the fruit stand this week than any other week

options.label: J
options.text: Week 4, because the number of pineapples was less than the expected number of customers

visual_elements: Table with two rows: Number of Pineapples and Number of Expected Customers; and four columns: Week 1 (110 pineapples, 50 customers), Week 2 (150 pineapples, 150 customers), Week 3 (200 pineapples, 40 customers), Week 4 (25 pineapples, 50 customers).
difficulty_rationale: Requires comparison of two sets of numerical data over multiple weeks and understanding the relationship between supply, demand, and likely pricing, involving reasoning beyond direct recall.
